title: 1 Chronicles 6:31–49
context: 1 Chronicles 6:31–49 names the musicians David appointed for the service of song after the ark came to rest in Jerusalem (compare 2 Samuel 6 and 1 Chronicles 15–16). Heman of the Kohathites stands in the center, Asaph of the Gershonites on his right, and Ethan of the Merarites on his left, each traced back to Levi. The other Levites serve in the tabernacle, while Aaron and his sons alone offer on the altars and make atonement, as Moses commanded. Psalm titles name an Asaph (Psalms 50, 73–83), a Heman (Psalm 88), and an Ethan (Psalm 89); interpreters discuss how far these are the same men. Both traditions share the central theme: God gave Israel ordered worship, in which song accompanied sacrifice and only the appointed priests made atonement.

verses.text: These are they whom David set over the service of song in the LORD’s house after the ark came to rest there.
verses.arminianNotes: These are the men David set over the service of song in the LORD’s house after the ark came to rest. Arminian readers see David organizing worship with care, and they see song as an important part of Israel’s response to God (compare 1 Chronicles 15–16).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see David’s arrangements as serving God’s appointed worship. Both traditions read the verse as connecting the musicians to the ark’s arrival in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6), which is shared ground.

verses.text: They ministered with song before the tabernacle of the Tent of Meeting until Solomon had built the LORD’s house in Jerusalem. They performed the duties of their office according to their order.
verses.arminianNotes: They served with song before the tabernacle until Solomon built the temple, performing their duties in order. Arminians see faithful, ordered service continuing through a time of transition.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress that the musicians served according to their appointed order. Both traditions see the verse as showing that worship was carried out with care and continuity from David to Solomon.

verses.text: These are those who served, and their sons. Of the sons of the Kohathites: Heman the singer, the son of Joel, the son of Samuel,
verses.arminianNotes: Heman the singer, a Kohathite, is traced as the son of Joel, the son of Samuel. Arminian readers see Samuel’s family continuing in God’s service through his grandson, even after his sons’ failures as judges.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s grace working across generations. Both traditions note that a Heman is named in the title of Psalm 88, and they discuss with caution whether he is the same man.

verses.text: the son of Elkanah, the son of Jeroham, the son of Eliel, the son of Toah,
verses.arminianNotes: Heman’s line continues through Elkanah, Jeroham, Eliel, and Toah. Arminians note that these names differ in places from the parallel list in 6:26–27, such as Eliel and Toah for Eliab and Nahath, and they name the difference without harmonizing it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and leave the differences as they stand. Both traditions read the verse as tracing Heman’s ancestry back through Samuel’s family.

verses.text: the son of Zuph, the son of Elkanah, the son of Mahath, the son of Amasai,
verses.arminianNotes: The line continues through Zuph, Elkanah, Mahath, and Amasai. Arminian readers recognize Zuph from 1 Samuel 1:1 and see the genealogy linking Heman to Samuel’s ancestors.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that the name Zuph also appears in the region named in 1 Samuel 9:5. Both traditions read the verse as a family record, and they avoid speculation beyond what the text gives.

verses.text: the son of Elkanah, the son of Joel, the son of Azariah, the son of Zephaniah,
verses.arminianNotes: The line continues through Elkanah, Joel, Azariah, and Zephaniah. Arminians note the repeated names Elkanah and Joel, which show how names were reused within families.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. The names here differ in places from 6:24, such as Joel and Azariah for Uriel and Uzziah, and both traditions name these differences without harmonizing them.

verses.text: the son of Tahath, the son of Assir, the son of Ebiasaph, the son of Korah,
verses.arminianNotes: The line continues through Tahath, Assir, Ebiasaph, and Korah. Arminian readers see Heman descending from Korah, whose rebellion was judged, which shows God’s mercy in using Korah’s descendants to lead worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s grace in giving Korah’s family an honored role. Both traditions note that several psalms are titled for the sons of Korah, which fits this family’s place among the singers.

verses.text: the son of Izhar, the son of Kohath, the son of Levi, the son of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: The line reaches Izhar, Kohath, Levi, and Israel. Arminians note that this verse names Izhar as Korah’s father, as Exodus 6:21 does, while 6:22 lists Amminadab, and they leave the difference unharmonized.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the line traced all the way to Israel himself. Both traditions read the verse as anchoring Heman’s service in God’s choice of Levi and of the whole nation.

verses.text: His brother Asaph, who stood on his right hand, even Asaph the son of Berechiah, the son of Shimea,
verses.arminianNotes: Asaph, Heman’s brother, stood on his right, the son of Berechiah, the son of Shimea. Arminian readers see Asaph as a leading musician, and they note that a number of psalms bear his name (Psalms 50, 73–83).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and hedge any identification with the psalm titles. Both traditions see the word brother here as describing a fellow Levite and colleague, since Asaph is from a different family.

verses.text: the son of Michael, the son of Baaseiah, the son of Malchijah,
verses.arminianNotes: Asaph’s line continues through Michael, Baaseiah, and Malchijah. Arminians see the genealogy giving Asaph a recognized place within the Gershonite branch of Levi.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as part of the record establishing each musician’s family. Both traditions treat the names as genealogical data without theological dispute.

verses.text: the son of Ethni, the son of Zerah, the son of Adaiah,
verses.arminianNotes: The line continues through Ethni, Zerah, and Adaiah. Arminian readers note that Zerah also appears in the Gershonite list in 6:21, though the surrounding names differ.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the two lists as distinct records. Both traditions name the differences between them without forcing agreement, and they read the verse as tracing Asaph’s family.

verses.text: the son of Ethan, the son of Zimmah, the son of Shimei,
verses.arminianNotes: The line continues through Ethan, Zimmah, and Shimei. Arminians note that this Ethan is an ancestor of Asaph and is different from the Ethan of 6:44, who leads the Merarite singers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as genealogy. Both traditions note that Zimmah appears in 6:20 as well, though the order of the names differs between the two lists.

verses.text: the son of Jahath, the son of Gershom, the son of Levi.
verses.arminianNotes: The line reaches Jahath, Gershom, and Levi. Arminian readers see Asaph’s family traced back to Levi, confirming his place among those God set apart for sanctuary service.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the full line establishing his legitimacy as a Levitical singer. Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about God’s ordering of worship.

verses.text: On the left hand their brothers the sons of Merari: Ethan the son of Kishi, the son of Abdi, the son of Malluch,
verses.arminianNotes: On the left stand the Merarites: Ethan son of Kishi, son of Abdi, son of Malluch. Arminians see each Levitical branch represented among the musicians, so that all three families share in leading Israel’s song.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. Many interpreters identify this Ethan with Jeduthun (compare 1 Chronicles 16:41; 25:1), though the text here does not say so, and both traditions hold the identification loosely.

verses.text: the son of Hashabiah, the son of Amaziah, the son of Hilkiah,
verses.arminianNotes: Ethan’s line continues through Hashabiah, Amaziah, and Hilkiah. Arminian readers see the genealogy establishing Ethan’s family within Merari, and they note that this Hilkiah is different from the high priest of 6:13.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as genealogical data. Both traditions note that the reuse of names across different families calls for care in reading these lists.

verses.text: the son of Amzi, the son of Bani, the son of Shemer,
verses.arminianNotes: The line continues through Amzi, Bani, and Shemer. Arminians see the record of faithful families whose names are kept even though nothing else is known about them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s faithfulness in remembering ordinary servants. Both traditions treat the verse as a straightforward link in the Merarite line.

verses.text: the son of Mahli, the son of Mushi, the son of Merari, the son of Levi.
verses.arminianNotes: The line reaches Mahli, Mushi, Merari, and Levi. Arminian readers note that elsewhere Mahli and Mushi are brothers (6:19), and they name the difference here without harmonizing it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and also leave the difference unharmonized. Both traditions read the verse as completing Ethan’s ancestry back to Levi.

verses.text: Their brothers the Levites were appointed for all the service of the tabernacle of God’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: The other Levites were appointed for all the service of the tabernacle. Arminians see every Levite having a share in God’s work, even those who did not lead song, which honors all kinds of service.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s appointment giving dignity to every task at the sanctuary. Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about faithful service in many forms.

verses.text: But Aaron and his sons offered on the altar of burnt offering, and on the altar of incense, for all the work of the most holy place, and to make atonement for Israel, according to all that Moses the servant of God had commanded.
verses.arminianNotes: Aaron and his sons alone offered on the altars of burnt offering and incense and made atonement for Israel, as Moses commanded. Arminian readers see atonement as God’s gracious provision for his people’s sin through the priests he appointed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress that atonement was carried out only as God commanded. Both traditions see the priests’ work as pointing forward to Christ’s final priesthood and sacrifice (compare Hebrews 9–10).
